name: Fatimid Caliphate
summary: An Ismaili Shi‘a caliphate that founded Cairo in 969 and its famous Al-Azhar mosque. It ruled North Africa, Egypt and the Levant until Saladin ended it in 1171.

knownFor.label: Founding of Cairo
knownFor.note: The Fatimids founded Cairo as their royal city.

knownFor.label: Al-Azhar
knownFor.note: A mosque founded in 970 that became one of the world’s oldest universities.

knownFor.label: Fatimid rock crystal
knownFor.note: Ewers carved from solid rock crystal, now treasures in European museums.

location.value: North Africa, then Egypt, the Levant and the Hejaz.

terrain.value: The Nile valley and delta, the North African coast, and the deserts between them.

climate.value: Low Nile floods caused famine in 1065–1072.

resources.value: Egypt’s grain and flax (for linen), and control of Red Sea trade.

disasters.value: A long famine in Egypt (1065–1072), caused by low Nile floods and unrest.

urbanisation.value: Founded Cairo in 969; it grew into one of the great cities of the Islamic world.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

disease.value: Repeated plague and famine, especially during the crisis of 1065–1072.

migration.value: Banu Hilal tribes moved west into North Africa.

economicBase.value: Rich Egyptian agriculture, linen weaving and trade between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean.

tradeRoutes.value: Red Sea routes to India and the Mediterranean trade with Italy and Byzantium, recorded in the Cairo Geniza documents.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold dinars of high purity, widely trusted; land taxes from Egypt.

inequality.value: The caliphal court and officials were wealthy.

governmentType.value: A hereditary caliphate led by Ismaili Shiʿa imams, ruling a mostly Sunni population.

keyRulers.value: al-Mahdi (909–934), al-Mu‘izz (953–975, conquered Egypt), al-Hakim (996–1021), al-Mustansir (1036–1094), vizier Badr al-Jamali.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

succession.value: Hereditary within the family; disputes split the Ismailis.

institutions.value: A large bureaucracy run by viziers; from the 1070s military viziers held real power.

stability.value: Stable until the army civil war and famine of the 1060s, after which viziers ruled.
stability.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

eliteConflict.value: Viziers versus caliphs, and rival army factions.

armyAndTech.value: A multi-ethnic army of Berber, Turkish and Sudanese troops, with a strong navy.

majorWars.value: Wars with the Abbasids and Byzantium; lost Syria to the Seljuks and Jerusalem to the Crusaders (1099).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

territoryChange.value: About 4.1 million km² at its height, from North Africa to Syria and the Hejaz.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Sunni Abbasids, the Seljuks and the Crusaders.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

inventions.value: Rock-crystal carving and lustreware pottery reached a high point.

openness.value: Some tolerance of Sunnis, Jews and Christians.

religion.value: Ismaili Shi‘a Islam as the state faith, ruling a mostly Sunni population with Christian and Jewish communities.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

languageWriting.value: Arabic, with Berber in North Africa and Coptic among Egyptian Christians.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

artsArchitecture.value: Al-Azhar Mosque, Cairo’s walls and gates.

socialStructure.value: Caliph and court, officials, soldiers, merchants, farmers; Christians and Jews served in government.

sharedIdentity.value: Ismaili faith and loyalty to the imam-caliph.

ideasReligions.value: Ismaili missionaries (da‘i) spread the faith as far as Yemen and Sindh.

riseSignals.value: Conquest of Egypt (969) and the founding of Cairo.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

peakPeriod.value: About 975–1050, when it ruled North Africa, Egypt, Syria and the holy cities of Arabia.

declineSignals.value: Famine and army civil war (1060s), Seljuk advances and the Crusades.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Fatimid Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Brett, The Fatimid Empire (2017)

outcome.value: Abolished by Saladin in 1171; succeeded by the Ayyubids.

sources.value: Chronicles and documents of the Cairo Geniza. Checked against Wikipedia (“Fatimid Caliphate”).

overallCertainty.value: Good. Well documented in Arabic chronicles and the Cairo Geniza.
